abstract: Hydrocephalus is a common and severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the ventricular system. Although its genetic basis is complex, recent studies have linked congenital hydrocephalus to defects in neural progenitor cell (NPC) maintenance, though how this results in ventricular obstruction remains unclear. Here we show that Notch signaling not only maintains NPCs within the ventricular zone (VZ) but also preserves the structural integrity of the developing ventricular system. Conditional ablation of the Notch effector Rbpj elicited premature differentiation of NPCs into neurons and disrupted VZ continuity. Cells lining the VZ lost their columnar organization, apical polarity, and adhesion contacts, breaking down the neuroepithelial layer and ependymal lining. This disruption obstructed CSF flow, causing hydrocephalus in neonatal mice. Pharmacological inhibition of Notch signaling in cortical spheroids similarly disrupted neural rosette formation, recapitulating aspects of the neuroepithelial defects observed in vivo. Collectively, our findings reveal critical roles for Notch signaling in preserving the walls of the ventricular system during brain development and provide insights into how disruptions to this pathway contribute to hydrocephalus.
